relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Naaman carries military honor and bodily vulnerability at the same time.
A captive girl, displaced by war, becomes the first bearer of healing knowledge.
She speaks hope into the household that holds her.
Her small sentence reaches a king.
Royal power answers with letters, wealth, and display.
The king of Israel is asked to do what no king can command.
Fear turns healing into suspected war.
Elisha redirects the crisis away from royal panic.
Naaman arrives expecting rank to open the prophet's door.
The instruction is ordinary: wash in the Jordan.
Naaman's imagined spectacle collides with a messenger and a river.
Pride compares waters and leaves in fury.
Servants bring him back toward the simple act.
He descends, dips, and receives renewed flesh.
Healing becomes confession and attempted gift.
Elisha refuses to sell what was freely given.
Naaman carries earth home as a sign of new allegiance.
He names the complexity of serving a king inside another temple.
The prophet answers complexity with peace.
Gehazi turns foreignness and gratitude into an opportunity for gain.
Naaman stops for the servant who runs after him.
A fabricated charitable need becomes the lie.
Naaman gives more than asked.
The goods disappear into concealment.
Gehazi stands before Elisha and denies movement.
The hidden transaction is exposed as a whole imagined estate of accumulation.
The story ends with disease transferred as judgment, a dangerous image that must not become stigma.

contemplative_note: The chapter's first prophet is the captive girl whose name the empire does not preserve. Healing crosses enemy lines through her voice, through servants' correction, and through a prophet who refuses payment. The wound of the story is that the girl remains captive even after the commander is made whole.
